entries.title: Kenya: Helicopter crash kills 7, including Ecuador spy boss
entries.summary: Six passengers — five US citizens and Ecuador's intel boss — all died in a remote area of Kenya on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed. Aviation accidents in Kenya have increased as tourism expands in the country.
entries.content:
United States of America

Kenya: Helicopter crash kills 7, including Ecuador spy boss

August 20, 2026

Six passengers — five US citizens and Ecuador's intel boss — all died in a remote area of Kenya on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed. Aviation accidents in Kenya have increased as tourism expands in the country.

Authorities in Kenya say that all seven people on board a safari helicopter — six passengers and a pilot — were killed on Wednesday when the chopper crashed in the foothills of the popular but remote tourist destination, Mount Ololokwe.

Kenya's Civil Aviation Authority said the group's Eurocopter EC130 B4 helicopter crashed at 9:13 a.m. (0613 GMT) after departing the Loisaba wildlife reserve on route to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu County north of the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, adding that an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the crash.

Video footage on social media showed the smoking wreckage of the helicopter strewn about, smoldering and burning in thickly wooded terrain.

What do we know about the victims of the Kenya crash?

The US State Department said that five of the six passengers killed were US citizens.

"The US Embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance," read a statement. "We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss."

An executive at Telemundo — a US-based Spanish-language television channel owned by Comcast/NBCUniversal — was reportedly among the victims.

Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of Ecuador's Strategic Intelligence Center was as well, and so was his wife, who also held US citizenship.

Sensi-Contugi, a former businessman, was a close friend and associate of Ecuador's right-wing President Daniel Noboa, who appointed him head of national intelligence in 2024.

"In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates," Ecuador's presidency said in a statement on X.

More accidents as tourism grows

Numerous travel companies offer helicopter tours to remote places like Mount Ololokwe.

But as Kenya's tourism sector has grown, so, too, has the frequency of helicopter crashes.

In February, another chopper went down in the wilderness, killing all six on board, including a parliamentarian.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: ICC slams US sanctions on court as 'flagrant attack'
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump's administration has ramped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), accusing it of being "politicized." The EU, France, Germany, Spain and Japan have defended the court.
entries.content:
United States of America

ICC slams US sanctions on court as 'flagrant attack'

August 19, 2026

US President Donald Trump's administration has ramped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), accusing it of being "politicized." The EU, France, Germany, Spain and Japan have defended the court.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) on Wednesday condemned US sanctions against the body's president, President Tomoko Akane of Japan, and trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal.

"These sanctions are a flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution," the Hague-based court said in a statement.

It said that the US sanctions "undermine the rule of law" and jeopardize the international legal order.

The court stressed it would "continue to fully discharge its mandate with independence and impartiality, in full accordance with the Rome Statute and in the interest of victims of international crimes."

Though the United States signed in 2000 the Rome Statute that established the court in 2002, it never ratified it and under President Donald Trump, Washington accuses the court of being "politicized."

The ICC prosecutes war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

EU, Japan show support for ICC

The European Union and several of its member states threw their weight behind the ICC.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa said they "stand firmly" with the court in identical statements on their X accounts.

"The ICC helps deliver justice to the victims of some of the world's most horrific crimes," they said. "To carry out this essential work, its judges and officials must be able to act independently and without external pressure."

Meanwhile, German Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig said she considered it "deeply distressing that it is the US of all countries that is launching a frontal attack on international criminal law."

She pointed out that the US helped establish the concept of international criminal law in the Nuremberg trials against members of Germany's Nazi regime.

"These US sanctions reflect contempt for the idea of the rule of law that cannot be reconciled with this tradition."

France also condemned the sanctions in a Wednesday statement.

"France condemns all ​of threats and means of coercion taken against the ​Court, its staff and the civil ⁠society organizations ​which support ​it," a statement from the spokesperson of the French Foreign Ministry said.

"France expresses its solidarity toward those magistrates targeted," it said.

Japanese Foreign Ministry Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura described the sanctions as "very unfortunate."

Japan is the biggest funder of the court.

The US sanctions were also condemned by the Netherlands, which hosts the court, and Spain, as well as the United Nations.

Why did the United States sanction the ICC?

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Tuesday, saying he was acting under authority of an executive order signed by President Trump.

He described the measure as part of an "unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court."

"These individuals," said Rubio, "have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC ."

Last month, Rubio said the Trump administration would step up its efforts to dismantle the ICC, including a diplomatic campaign for other countries to leave the court.

In 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

The move was condemned by the United States, with Trump accusing the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel." Like the US, Israel has also never ratified the Rome Statute and is therefore not an ICC state party.

The court also issued or planned to issue arrest warrants for several now deceased Hamas leading officials.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Ceuta: Madrid to transfer 500 vulnerable youths to mainland
entries.summary: Spanish officials have come up with a plan to transfer unaccompanied youth in the exclave Ceuta to mainland Spain. Mostly girls, they will be placed in foster homes as well as under government care.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Spanish officials have come up with a plan to transfer unaccompanied youth in the exclave Ceuta to mainland Spain. Mostly girls, they will be placed in foster homes as well as under government care.

Spanish immigration and youth services officials have come up with a plan to transfer roughly 500 particularly vulnerable unaccompanied youths from the North African Spanish exclave of Ceuta to mainland Spain.

Spain's Ministry of Youth and Children says the plan has a mechanism that will allow "child protection organizations to take in and care for the most vulnerable individuals — including girls — in adapted facilities on the mainland, without the need to transfer custody to [regional authorities]."

What else do we know about the measure?

On Wednesday, Spain's Migration Minister Elma Saiz told public broadcaster RNE that Madrid is working with Ceuta and Spain's regional governments to organize the transfer and placement of the children, mainly girls, in foster homes as well as under government care.

Spain's EFE news agency quoted government officials saying that a royal decree would establish "the binding and solidarity-based reception of minors by all regions."

Migration Minister Saiz emphasized the fact that the "overriding welfare of the children" must be protected at all cost.

UNICEF Spain's Lara Contreras said the approach would see Ceuta retain legal guardianship of the girls until they were transferred to child protection organizations "willing to take them in" on the Spanish mainland.

Contreras said that 97 of the 500 girls selected — aged 9 to 17 — have already been moved to improved facilities and will be transferred as soon as possible.

Contreras says it is "urgent" that authorities properly identify unaccompanied children and denounced the fact that "hundreds of them are wandering the streets alone, in unsanitary conditions."

What is the situation in Ceuta?

The children are among the roughly 80,000 individuals who crossed into Ceuta from Morocco on July 30 in hopes of starting a better life in Europe.

Though most migrants have since returned to Morocco, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska recently said that around 5,000 remain in Ceuta.

Spain's national police have reportedly identified 2,168 unaccompanied minors living on the streets since the border crossing and handed them over to local authorities on July 30.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Zambia: Mundubile seeks to overturn election result in court
entries.summary: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile's party alleges shots were fired during a raid of his house on election night. UN rights chief Volker Türk called for Zambia to stop arresting people "arbitrarily."
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia: Mundubile seeks to overturn election result in court

August 19, 2026

Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile's party alleges shots were fired during a raid of his house on election night. UN rights chief Volker Türk called for Zambia to stop arresting people "arbitrarily."

Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile said on Wednesday that he plans to challenge the results of this month's presidential election result in court.

Zambia's electoral commission declared incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema the winner of the election on Tuesday, giving him a second five-year term. He has been in power since 2021.

The election was marred by accusations of interference and by arrests of opposition figures.

What did Mundubile say about his push to challenge the election result?

While announcing his intention to legally challenge the result, Mundubile pointed to irregularities and other issues with the election.

"Our campaign ​has documented serious irregularities, inconsistencies and circumstances ​surrounding the conduct, counting, transmission and declaration of results", Mundubile said in a statement issued from an undisclosed location.

The politician had earlier said he was under protection due to threats.

Mundubile received 38% of the vote on Tuesday, while Hichilema took 60%, according to the electoral commission.

While the vote itself was largely peaceful, some 11 people — including leading figures in the opposition — were arrested on the night of the election. The government said that the arrests were part of a raid against "militia activity.”

Mundubile's National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) said that shots were fired during the raid of the opposition figure's home. The party also denied any ties to militias.

Vote counting was also suspended for multiple hours on Friday after the electoral commission reported attacks against polling officials and theft of some ballots.

UN rights chief calls for Zambia to halt arrests, EU mission notes irregularity

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, said he was concerned by reports of arrests of opposition members.

In a statement, he urged authorities "to stop arresting people arbitrarily and to uphold fully the due process rights of all those detained."

Meanwhile, an electoral observer mission for the European Union raised concerns around transparency.

"Observers reported extended breaks during the results tabulation process in almost half of observations, as the returning officers seemed to wait and receive instructions from... headquarters before announcing results," the mission said.

Edited by: Mark Hallam

entries.title: Liberia says it's taking in 1,200 third-country US deportees
entries.summary: The government in Monrovia says the first batch of 20 people should arrive in Liberia on Thursday. The Trump administration has been seeking countries to take people it cannot send back to their countries of origin.
entries.content:
United States of America

Liberia says it's taking in 1,200 third-country US deportees

August 19, 2026

The government in Monrovia says the first batch of 20 people should arrive in Liberia on Thursday. The Trump administration has been seeking countries to take people it cannot send back to their countries of origin.

Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the United States in the next 12 months, the government said this week. 

It said that the first group of 20 were expected to arrive on Thursday.

Donald Trump's administration has recently struck several deals with African countries to take in people it cannot legally send back to their home countries — typically because of US court orders ruling that doing so would put them in danger. 

What did Liberia say about the agreement?

"Liberia intends to accept up to 1,200 persons to be transferred from the United States of America within a year," the Liberian government said in a statement published on Tuesday.

It said that the people would be received "as guests" and that they would be "free to depart the country when they so desire" or to apply for asylum.

The government's statement said the deportees "will include citizens or nationals of ‌African ​and Western Hemisphere countries who are medically authorized to travel."

It said that the deal did not involve a quid pro quo with the US and that it was not demanding and had not received any direct compensation.

However, it also said that it would receive "support to help manage the program and strengthen its migration system more broadly," without elaborating.

The statement also referenced Liberia's 19th century history as a refuge for freed slaves from the US, and its "long history of accepting ⁠people seeking refuge from political ​and other crises."

Why is the US looking for support of this kind from African countries?

The announcement follows around a year after Liberian President Joseph Boakai visited the White House among a group of African leaders and held talks with Trump. 

Seeking a way to deport would-be migrants that it cannot send back to their countries of origin — very often because of US courts ruling that doing so would put them at risk of torture or other abuses — the Trump administration has been seeking agreements with third countries willing to take some of the people.

The US government has defended such agreements as lawful, although some rights groups and advocates have said the details are often opaque and that many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.

Beyond Monrovia's description, no information was immediately available on where exactly the deportees hailed from.

Other African countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Central African Republic, Equatorian Guinea, Cameroon, Ghana and Sierra Leone have reached similar accords with the US. 

The EU is currently looking into somewhat comparable plans that would allow member states to send rejected asylum seekers to so-called "return hubs" in third countries as part of bilateral or multilateral agreements, provided various conditions were met.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine
entries.summary: More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.
entries.content:
Africa

CAR: Scores killed in landslide at illegal gold mine

August 19, 2026

More than 100 workers may have been killed in a landslide at an illegal mine near the Central African Republic's border with Cameroon, say authorities. More miners are trapped and hope for their survival is fading.

Authorities in the western part of the Central African Republic (CAR) say dozens of laborers were killed Tuesday afternoon when a landslide buried them at the illegal Zamboye mining site near the Cameroon border — about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the town of Baboua.

Death tolls have ranged from "at least 30" initially to "over 100," with local authorities saying the window for survival is quickly closing for the many miners still buried at the site.

Video uploaded to social media platforms showed bodies churning in earth as the landslide lunges into the open-pit site beneath, burying everything in its path.

Frantic rescue activities continued on Wednesday with reports of mud-covered young men and women pulling bodies from the mine's collapsed entrance, as still more screamed for help.

"The collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating," was given as the cause of the collapse by the Baboua public prosecutor's office, which also announced that an investigation had been launched.

CAR government spokesman Evariste Ngamana expressed sympathy and pledged the government was "working hard to provide relief and assistance."

What is the state of CAR's 'artisanal' mines?

Improvised "artisanal" mines in the gold-rich region are often illegal and shoddily built, following limited or no safety standards whatsoever.

That means the thousands of laborers who use their hands to mine for gold every day, put their lives at risk each time they enter one.

Serious accidents are a regular occurrence and these are usually very deadly.

Dozens of miners have been killed in landslides in the area since the beginning of the year.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Germany condemns Israeli minister's call to 'remove' Palestinians
entries.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has denounced a call by Israel's far-right security minister to carry out "targeted killings" of Palestinians in Gaza. The outrage spans the entire political spectrum.
entries.content:
Germany

German lawmakers condemn Israeli minister's Gaza remarks

August 19, 2026

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has denounced a call by Israel's far-right security minister to carry out "targeted killings" of Palestinians in Gaza. The outrage spans the entire political spectrum.

"I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza," said Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, on Monday, sparking worldwide outrage.

The hard-liner in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Cabinet also described exactly what he had in mind: Every night, 30 or 40 Palestinians should be "removed." Ben-Gvir emphasized that he was not only referring to militant Palestinians who posed an immediate threat, adding that there are people in the Gaza Strip who do not deserve to live.

On Wednesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz denounced the statement made by the controversial Israeli politician. "The chancellor strongly condemns Minister Ben-Gvir's inhumane statements, which violate international law — they are unacceptable," said a government spokesperson in Berlin. Merz is officially on vacation.

The spokesperson also criticized Israel's plans to further accelerate settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Merz is following the latest developments "with great concern."

The spokesperson said there must be no further steps toward annexation, adding: "As the occupying power, Israel must treat Palestinians with dignity, protect their property and ensure public administration and humanitarian aid."

Vice Chancellor Klingbeil: 'A line has truly been crossed'

Merz's deputy from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, had already called for consequences on Tuesday.

"These are statements that we, as the federal government, cannot accept in any way," he told the private TV station Sat1. Klingbeil said that sanctions are being discussed at the European level, adding: "This must now be looked at very seriously." Despite all its solidarity with the state of Israel, Germany must not remain silent, he stressed. A line has now "truly been crossed."

Hildegard Bentele, a German member of the European Parliament from the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), also supports sanctions against Ben-Gvir, telling DW on Tuesday that she had been calling for them for a year.

"Eliminating individuals is unacceptable to us in Europe," she emphasized.

Many countries have imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir

Several countries have already imposed entry bans on Ben-Gvir, including Australia, France, the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Norway and the Netherlands.

Jürgen Hardt, the foreign policy spokesperson for the conservative parliamentary group in Germany's lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, also supports the call for European Union sanctions against Ben-Gvir. 

"The EU should sanction him as a statement on the universal validity of human dignity and human rights," Hardt told the news magazine Politico. Hardt said he is convinced that an Israeli Cabinet without Ben-Gvir would bring Europe and Israel closer together again.

Calls for sanctions and a halt to arms exports to Israel

The environmentalist Green Party, an opposition party in the German parliament, has also demanded harsh consequences.

"I urge the federal government to impose an entry ban on this man and to advocate for similar sanctions to be imposed at the European level as well," Green Party leader Franziska Brantner told Politico.

This is not the first time Ben-Gvir has drawn attention for his appalling calls for violence against Palestinians, Brantner emphasized. She also called for Germany to follow the example of other countries and impose sanctions: "It's time for Germany to join these nations."

Lea Reisner, a politician from the socialist Left Party, went further on Deutschlandfunk public radio, calling for a halt to all German arms exports to Israel.

Josef Schuster: Ben-Gvir's comments 'deeply shameful and irresponsible'

Germany's Central Council of Jews in Germany also reacted with horror to Ben-Gvir's call for mass killings of Palestinians. The president of the Central Council, Josef Schuster, told the Catholic News Agency that Ben-Gvir's statements were diametrically opposed to Jewish values and damage Israel's reputation.

"Itamar Ben-Gvir's behavior is deeply shameful and irresponsible," said Schuster, adding that it illustrates the danger posed by far-right forces.

Kirsten Fehrs, chair of the Council of the Protestant Church in Germany, described Ben-Gvir's statements on the social media platform Threads as an "attack on humanity." The bishop stressed that there must be a shared conviction across religions that every human being possesses inalienable dignity because they are made in God's image.

"No one can bestow this dignity, and no one can take it away," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India 'Cockroach' movement takes aim at government schools
entries.summary: The student protest movement is turning its grassroots network into a nationwide campaign to audit neglected government schools and pressure authorities to act.
entries.content:
India

India 'Cockroach' movement takes aim at government schools

August 19, 2026

The student protest movement is turning its grassroots network into a nationwide campaign to audit neglected government schools and pressure authorities to act.

The student protest movement in India known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) scored a major victory in July after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down following weeks of demonstrations in Delhi.

Now, the movement is aiming its campaign for accountability at improving India's government schools.

Last week on India's Independence Day, the CJP launched a nationwide campaign asking citizens to inspect government schools, document what is missing and pressure local authorities to fix basic facilities.

Dubbed "Fix the Schools," the campaign aims to mobilize citizens to identify problems locally and make them public.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke launched a campaign in the Indian state of Maharashtra from his native village in Hingoli district. He spoke with students and documented what he said were broken windows, lack of clean drinking water, missing classroom benches and unusable bathrooms.

"No matter which political party ruled, nobody worked for government schools in states. Now there is a need, and we can make them work by asking questions," said Dipke.

Government officials did not respond to DW's requests for comment on the CJP's accusations.

What does the plan call for?

The CJP has prepared assessment forms that parents, students and residents can use to document issues with local government schools. They are being asked to record video evidence, complete the assessment and send the material to CJP.

The organization plans to compile the reports into a public record of neglected schools and use them to pressure local authorities to respond.

The CJP has said the campaign will focus on five basic requirements: functioning toilets, electricity, clean drinking water, classroom benches and the quality of midday meals.

One element is to publicly recognize village heads who improve their local schools. The CJP plans to use before-and-after evidence to highlight villages where conditions have improved.

The organization has set an initial target of auditing at least 100 rural government schools over the next two months and pressing authorities to act on the findings.

CJP seeks to expand support

The youth-led CJP began in May as a campaign calling for accountability over a scandal involving a highly competitive university entrance exam. The news that the question sheet had been leaked ahead of the exam date in early May exposed long-running grievances over privileged access for some students.

Fueled by millions of young followers on social media, the movement soon tapped into wider frustrations over unemployment, shrinking opportunities and an education system many young Indians believe has failed them.

After the education minister stepped down, and the government promised steps toward accountability for those involved in the exam paper leaks, the CJP has shifted focus.

However, to be effective in localities around India, the youth-based movement, which has initially mainly been based in Delhi, will need to broaden its appeal.

This comes as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day address, placed youth power at the center of his vision for a developed India.

India's youth a political force

Aruna Roy, a prominent Indian social activist and former civil servant who helped lead a grassroots movement that resulted in India's landmark Right to Information Act in 2005, said the CJP's campaign could tap into a wider constituency of young people seeking greater accountability.

"The demands at Jantar Mantar resonated with young people across the country," Roy said, referring to the location in central Delhi where the protests were based.

"It was, in many cases, a spontaneous revolt against the state for failing to deliver on promises affecting their education, employment and future," Roy told DW.

"When young people have decided to fight against the destruction of their dreams, they are formidable," she added.

CJP opens door for 'citizen audits'

Responsibility for government school infrastructure is spread across state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies, while conditions vary widely across India.

The CJP's new campaign is a test of whether the movement's ability to mobilize students, volunteers, money and public attention outside traditional political structures can be sustained beyond last month's high-profile victory.

Amrita Johri, an activist and transparency advocate, said CJP had tapped into larger issues with India's education system.

"Millions of young people have lost precious years and resources because of repeated failures to ensure fair examinations, with little accountability for those responsible," Johri told DW.

"Every government school should publicly disclose its spending, infrastructure, teacher vacancies and midday meal provision," Johri said.

"The CJP can make this meaningful by training volunteers to systematically document problems and follow up, while helping local communities use tools such as the Right to Information to demand change," she added.

Social activist Roy said citizen audits could turn public anger into sustained pressure for accountability.

"Citizen audits are vital because they expose corruption and the arbitrary use of power and bring people into the struggle for accountability," she said.

The campaign gives parents and residents a direct role in documenting what they see around them. CJP has said they do not need to wait for an official inspection to identify a broken toilet, a school without drinking water or classrooms without basic furniture.

What comes next?

The first test will be whether its target of 100 schools produces visible changes, and whether the model can be replicated beyond the places where CJP already has organizers and supporters.

The organization has also indicated that it could extend the citizen audit model to public healthcare facilities, widening its focus from education to other basic government services.

N. Sai Balaji, former president of the All India Students' Association, said CJP was broadening the fight over education reform and creating the possibility of convergence with student movements already campaigning on higher education.

"The two will meet, and there is a clear synergy. The impact will be felt as the momentum builds," Balaji told DW.

For a movement that began with a protest over examination irregularities, the next phase is less about taking to the streets and more about documenting what citizens encounter in their everyday lives.

"We have built a new parliament, a new PM house. Why have we not been able to build new schools in our villages? Do we not consider the children of farmers and laborers the future of our country?" asked CJP leader Dipke in a video message.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Why the US is going after the International Criminal Court
entries.summary: Marco Rubio, Donald Trump's secretary of state, has announced sanctions against two members of the International Criminal Court, including its president. Rubio's pressure on the court has far-reaching consequences.
entries.content:
United States of America

Why the US is going after the International Criminal Court

August 19, 2026

Marco Rubio, Donald Trump's secretary of state, has announced sanctions against two members of the International Criminal Court, including its president. Rubio's pressure on the court has far-reaching consequences.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took aim at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Tuesday, calling it "corrupt and fatally politicized" and claiming it has "maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate."

He announced sanctions against the ICC president, Tomoko Akane of Japan, and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal. The sanctions include freezing of their US-held bank assets and largely cutting them off from the US financial system.

The ICC has been holding individuals accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity since 2002. The court is based in The Hague, just like the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is part of the United Nations and settles disputes between states.

Unlike the ICJ, the ICC has 125 members, not all 193 UN member states. The US, Russia and China are among the countries that have not joined, along with several states in Asia and North Africa.

Rubio had recently threatened to dismantle the court "brick by brick." In a statement in July, the State Department outlined a number of measures Washington is considering as part of its campaign against the court. These include visa restrictions on ICC staff and tougher sanctions targeting the court and affiliated organizations. It also suggested increased scrutiny of countries "that refuse to reject the ICC's illegitimate authority" while continuing to receive US assistance.

The US has clashed with the ICC before. But legal experts around the world say Washington's latest escalation marks a significant shift.

How Washington is piling pressure onto The Hague

"What the US and Marco Rubio have now essentially done is make public something that has been going on for more than a year," Andreas Schüller, co-director of the International Crimes and Legal Accountability Program at the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) in Berlin, told DW in July.

"The US has been using various forms of diplomatic pressure against other countries in an effort to change their positions, and in some cases their voting behavior, toward the ICC," he added.

"The fact that it is now being declared a campaign shows that it is being pursued strategically, that it is broader in scope, and that other countries — including those that are not ICC members — are also being brought on board to help apply pressure."

A court to ensure no perpetrator can escape justice

The US is not a member of the International Criminal Court, meaning crimes committed on US soil do not fall under its jurisdiction. But the ICC can prosecute alleged atrocities committed in member states — a principle that led, for example, to arrest warrants being issued for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The ICC has its roots in the lessons of history. The Nuremberg trials after World War II, which put leading Nazi figures on trial, marked the birth of modern international criminal law. After war crimes tribunals were set up in the 1990s following the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia and the genocide in Rwanda, calls for a permanent court gained momentum.

For Kai Ambos, an international law expert at the University of Göttingen, the issue comes down to "the fundamental question of accountability" — whether in Ukraine, Iran or Gaza.

"It cannot be that such serious crimes are committed, regardless of the conflict, and those primarily responsible — above all government leaders and other figures in power — go unpunished. Nothing happens. That is unacceptable for victims, but ultimately for all of us," Ambos told DW before the recent US sanctions.

Should US citizens be in the dock?

In a short video address in July, Rubio said the court posed a threat to the entire US legal system.

"Border Patrol agents removing violent criminals from our country. American Marines risking their lives to defend our nation. … If we do nothing, they would all be left at the mercy of foreign judges thousands of miles away," he said.

No case against US citizens is currently pending before the ICC. The actions of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers take place largely on US territory, where the court has no jurisdiction.

The situation is different when it comes to the targeted killings of alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean: Former ICC prosecutor Luis Moreno Ocampo described them in November as potential crimes against humanity.

How can the court withstand the pressure?

Ambos fears that the so-called "chilling effect" could intensify — meaning, for example, that ICC prosecutors might become more cautious when dealing with US suspects. "And then there is the problem of overcompliance with sanctions — meaning that companies outside the US may also say: We will no longer work with the institution because it could put our business in the US at risk."

In 2025, the US State Department had already imposed a series of sanctions on the ICC and individual judges. The court responded by reducing its reliance on the US, replacing, for example, Microsoft Office software with a German open-source alternative.

ECCHR expert Schüller sees many small ways for member states to support the court. "If medium-sized powers and smaller states join forces against the US and come together as a pillar of support for international institutions, pushing back against this pressure, then that is the most important thing," he said.

The EU backed the ICC immediately after Rubio's previous threats in July. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul also defended the court, saying it makes the world "safer and more just."

Ironically, the US Senate held a similar view in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In a resolution, it described the ICC as "an international tribunal that seeks to uphold the rule of law" and welcomed its investigations into Russia. One of the co-sponsors of the resolution, introduced by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, was none other than current US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

This article was originally written in German. This version was originally published on July 17, 2026, and updated on August 19, 2026, to reflect the recent US sanctions.

entries.title: Germany's rusting sea munitions are a toxic time bomb
entries.summary: Toxic chemicals from decades-old bombs are contaminating marine life in German waters. Scientists warn that the window to remove the weapons is closing.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Toxic chemicals from decades-old bombs are contaminating marine life in German waters. Scientists warn that the window to remove the weapons is closing.

Beneath the seas off Germany's northern coast, vast quantities of bombs and other weapons are slowly rusting away.

They are part of an estimated 1.6 million metric tons of conventional munitions in the North Sea and Baltic Sea, a legacy of two world wars and the mass disposal of weapons after 1945.

How old weapons pose a new threat

For decades, the material was largely left alone unless it posed an explosive danger. But as metal casings corrode, a different problem is emerging.

Some weapons are remnants of fighting: mines, unexploded bombs and ammunition lost at sea. But huge quantities were deliberately dumped after Nazi Germany surrendered in 1945, as the Allies disposed of the country's vast arsenal.

What was once regarded as an explosive hazard has now become an environmental one.

"It's clear that due to corrosion of these items, compounds enter the marine ecosystem and enter marine life," Kiel University toxicologist Edmund Maser told DW. "It turned out that these compounds are toxic and carcinogenic, both for human life and also for marine life," he said.

Among the most toxic compounds in the old weapons is trinitrotoluene, or TNT, a military explosive. Jörn Scharsack of Germany's Thünen Institute of Fisheries Ecology looked for evidence of it in dab fish.

"We find TNT in the fish, or let's say, metabolization, degradation products of TNT," he said.

The quantities are tiny — measured in nanograms — and not every fish contains detectable levels. But researchers repeatedly find the compounds around old munitions hotspots. "It's low. But it's there."

How toxic munitions are affecting marine life

So far, the contamination does not appear to be making fish acutely sick.

"The fish look healthy when we take them out. They do not have more diseases in terms of viral, bacterial, parasite diseases," Scharsack told DW. There is, however, one recurring abnormal finding.

"What we see is tumors, so tumors in the liver. That pops up again and again."

Maser's group has also found munitions compounds in fish, as well as mussels.

Together with the Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) in Bremerhaven, his team found liver abnormalities in more than 50% of fish living around some munitions dumping grounds and wrecks, compared with normal rates of just 1–2%.

Mussels, meanwhile, showed biochemical signs of oxidative stress. As TNT is metabolized, highly reactive forms of oxygen can damage proteins, lipids and even DNA. "This can be a step towards cancer," said Maser.

And the contamination does not stop with fish and mussels.

Maser's team has also detected TNT-related compounds in tissue samples from two stranded whales, showing that the chemicals are reaching animals at the top of the marine food web.

"That means that these compounds have arrived in top predators," he said.

Are Germany's sea munitions dangerous to humans?

That raises the obvious question: If TNT-related compounds are reaching top predators, are people who eat seafood at risk?

For now, both scientists say the answer is no.

Whales face more constant exposure through prey and surrounding water, while humans are exposed only occasionally through seafood.

"One would need to eat lots of fish to really reach a level where it's getting dangerous," said Scharsack. "I'm still going swimming. I'm still eating fish."

The concern is what happens as the munitions continue to deteriorate.

"I would say it's likely to get worse if we look at the ongoing corrosion of the munitions," Scharsack said.

"The shells are corroding. More and more of the toxic substances are lying open, exposed to the water."

The problem appears worse in the Baltic than the North Sea because weaker currents and water exchange allow leaking pollutants to linger rather than disperse.

What mussels reveal about TNT contamination

Maser's research suggests this may already be happening. His team examined archived mussels dating back to 1985 and found TNT-related contamination increasing steadily from around 2000 through 2022.

"It's low, but it's increasing," he said. "And we expect that over the coming decades, maybe two or three or four decades, we will have concentrations that could maybe harm the human seafood consumer."

Marine life is already under pressure from what Maser described as a "whole cocktail" of human-made pollutants, including microplastics, pesticides and pharmaceutical compounds. Munitions add another contaminant to that mix.

Unlike many of those pollutants, which are already dispersed through the oceans, bombs and mines remain physical objects that can be salvaged and disposed of.

And the window will not stay open forever.

Germany has long removed munitions posing an immediate danger, but only recently began pilot projects for systematic clearance to prevent environmental harm.

"The topic has been ignored for decades. Nobody wanted to talk about it," Scharsack said.

What are the challenges in clearing munitions?

In a study published in July, GEOMAR researcher Torsten Frey and colleagues identified 484 known or potential munitions piles in two areas of the Baltic Sea. But of the estimated 1.6 million tons of munitions in German waters, around 1.5 million tons have yet to be mapped, Frey told DW.

Recovering the munitions from known locations is no longer the main obstacle, Frey said, with specialist companies able to clear large quantities relatively quickly. "The bottleneck is the disposal and destruction of the recovered munitions."

Germany is developing an offshore treatment platform to help increase disposal capacity. "This will be a marathon, not a sprint," said Frey.

Even clearance will leave small pieces of explosive behind, some no larger than "a sugar cube." Maser is investigating whether marine bacteria and fungi could eventually break down these residues into CO2 and water.

The work is still at the laboratory stage and Maser stresses that it cannot replace physical clearance.

"We need more of these platforms," he said. "We need to start as early as possible."

"If we wait maybe 40 years, then maybe all these metal cases are corroded and we have then no chance to get these munition compounds out of the water," said Maser. "This is why we should act now."



Edited by: Rosalie Delaney
